items.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995
items.q: I don’t know whether that was Clark Terry’s words but he says first you imitate, then you assimilate, and lastly then you [innovate].

ctx.x: Sometimes the artist is the last one to see his money am I right?

Absolutely. We create it but it’s a business. And learn that it’s a business. I think kids know that today. They’re much hipper about it. But I kind of regret that I was much older before I found out things like that, I wasn’t into it. I just wanted to play, I wanted to play. And I can’t play this thing that I hear in my head, I’ve got to keep playing. But I don’t think there are any shortcuts. I don’t know whether that was Clark Terry’s words but he says first you imitate, then you assimilate, and lastly then…
All right. We want to thank Derek Smith for joining us on this wonderful cruise, and say goodbye now for the Hamilton Jazz Archive.

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Derek for – maybe he might have subbed for a time or two, but he never was one of the regulars that played with us.

ctx.x: Derek Smith? Did you use him?

Derek for – maybe he might have subbed for a time or two, but he never was one of the regulars that played with us. It was a great group. Right now, people still tell me that’s one of the greatest groups that ever came down the pike. We had a beautiful repertoire of a variety of things. We played anything from the swift, hip stuff to the old, lowdown, greasy, grimy blues. One of the things that we used to enjoy very much doing was an old tune called The Battle Hymn of the Republic. It went [Terry sings] “Glory,…
Did you have Miroslav Vitous in that band?
